Chapter 7. Sacca (truthfulness)

“By this truth may there be well-being, the poison destroyed, may Yaññadatta live.”

Sacca (truthfulness1) is being truthful through body, speech and mind. To reach the four noble truths, a person has to be truthful about himself: truthful about what is really there in the mind. Kusala (good) is kusala (good) and akusala (bad) is akusala (bad), whether it arises2 in oneself or in someone else.

Sacca (truthfulness) not deceiving3 in speech What it is What it does finds out what is really so How it shows itself excellence What it needs honesty Bean soup. The Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets) compares deceitful speech to bean soup. When bean soup is cooked, some beans are cooked and some are not, and whoever eats it now and then bites on a hard one. Speech is like that. When a person talks a great deal, some false words may be mixed in. Or everything he says may be true, from the first word to the last. Only paññā (wisdom) knows which it is.

The Ten Perfections for Young Readers  ·  34

a cooked bean: a true word a hard bean: a deceptive word Only paññā (wisdom) knows which is which, and it knows from inside, not from outside.

bean soup When a person talks a great deal, some deceptive words may be mixed in.

“when one cooks beansoup, some beans are cooked while others are not cooked”

Truthful to the Triple Gem. Truthfulness begins with truthfulness towards the Tiratana (the Triple Gem: the Buddha, the Dhamma, his teaching, and the Saṅgha, his enlightened4 disciples5). When a person sees a Buddha statue, is there respect for the Buddha’s qualities, or is there a request for favours: protection, possessions, praise? That question shows how truthful the citta (consciousness6) is. Being truthful to the Dhamma (the teaching) means studying it in order to understand it, not in order to gain anything.

“Thus have I heard.” After the Buddha’s passing, five hundred arahant (fully enlightened) monks7 met to recite8 the whole teaching together. This meeting is called the First Council9. The Venerable Ānanda, who had been the Buddha’s attendant and had heard all his discourses10, sat down in the teacher’s seat to recite them. Some devas (heavenly beings11) thought that Ānanda must now have become a Buddha himself. Ānanda knew their thoughts, and he would not accept praise for a quality he did not have. So he began with the words evaṃ me sutaṃ (thus have I heard): “On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Wood, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park”. By those words he showed that he was only a disciple, repeating what he had heard. The five hundred arahants (fully enlightened ones) and thousands of devas (heavenly beings) cried “sādhu” (good), the earth trembled and flowers fell from the sky.

Those words still open every discourse in the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets). The Buddha is gone, but the Dhamma (the teaching) itself is now the teacher.

Not by water. On cold winter nights, a crowd of ascetics12 were plunging into the river and climbing out again, believing that this made them pure. The Buddha saw them and said:

Not by water is one pure, tho’ many folk bathe here. In whom is truth and dhamma, he is pure and he’s a brāhmin.

Light is the enemy of darkness, and knowledge is the enemy of ignorance13. Water does not destroy the roots of evil, so water cannot wash evil away. If it could, the fish and the tortoises, the cows and the buffaloes would all be pure. What makes a person pure is truth.

How the Bodhisatta practised. The commentary14 gives a short rule for the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-tobe): “He should work energetically for the welfare of beings, be capable of enduring15 everything whether desirable or undesirable, and should speak without deception.” It adds: “He should suffuse all beings with universal16 loving-kindness17 and compassion18.” People usually have mettā (loving-kindness) for good people and not for bad ones. But when someone looks down on a person who does wrong, the citta (consciousness) of the one who looks down is akusala (bad), the same kind as the wrongdoer19’s. The

commentary also says: “Without truthfulness, virtue, etc., is impossible, and there can be no practice in accordance with one’s vows.” The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) made a vow to become a Buddha. A vow can only be kept by someone who is firm in truth.

Hārita, who would not lie. In one life the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was born into a very rich family, and because of his golden skin they called him Hārita. When his parents died he thought: I too will die. So he gave away his wealth and became a recluse20 in the Himālaya, where he reached deep calm of mind and the higher powers.

One day he came to Vārāṇasī (a city in India). The king had faith in him, built him a dwelling in the royal park and fed him from the palace. He lived there twelve years. Then the king went away to settle trouble on the border and asked the queen to look after the recluse. One day, when Hārita came to the palace, he saw the queen, and the kilesa (defilements21) that had lain quiet in him for thousands of aeons22 rose up like a poisonous snake out of a box. His calm of mind vanished, he could not find sati (mindfulness23), and he did wrong.

The whole city talked about it. The king would not believe it. When he came home he went to the park, bowed to the recluse, and asked whether the rumour24 was true, adding that he took it to be false. Hārita thought: if I say I did not do it, the king will believe me. But in this world there is no surer foundation than truthful speech, and someone who forsakes the truth cannot become a Buddha. In some lives a Bodhisatta (a Buddha-to-be) may break other rules, but he never tells a lie. So Hārita answered:

The rumours, great King, you have heard are true. Infatuated25 by the objects26 of delusion27, I have done wrong.

The king praised his honesty and urged him to throw off the lust28 that was destroying him. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) came back to himself and said:

Sense pleasures are blinding, they cause much suffering29. They injure gravely30. I shall look for the root of sensuousness31, I shall cut down lust with its bonds.

He regained jhāna (deep calm of mind), went back to the forest, and at the end of his life was reborn32 in the brahma (highest heavenly) world. The Buddha told this story to a monk who wanted to leave the Order after seeing a beautifully dressed woman. He said that even he, as the recluse Hārita, with all his powers, had fallen because of that kind of defilement. “Why should a strong wind that strikes Mount Sineru not carry off a withered leaf?” Nobody is as steady as Mount Sineru (the great mountain at the centre of the world); people are withered leaves, and the wind is lobha (attachment33), dosa (anger) and moha (ignorance). When the Buddha had explained the truths, that monk became an arahant (fully enlightened).

Kaṇhadīpāyana and the snake. In another life the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was the seer34 Dīpāyana. For more than fifty years he was unhappy as a recluse, and he told no one. He stayed only because he feared that people would say he had left his wealth and now wanted it back. He kept his hiri

(shame) and ottappa (fear of blame), and he stayed, sometimes with tears running down his face. He was called Kaṇhadīpāyana (Black Dīpāyana) because he had sat all night beside a wounded friend, and the drops of blood dried black on his body.

One day a friend came to visit with his wife and little son, Yaññadatta. The boy threw a ball, it rolled near a poisonous snake, and when the boy felt for it the snake bit him. He fell to the ground. His parents were in agony35, and the seer with them. Then Dīpāyana made a saccakiriyā (an assertion of truth). He said that for only seven days had he lived the holy life gladly, and that for more than fifty years he had lived it unwillingly, and by that truth might the poison be destroyed and Yaññadatta live. The boy stood up and was well. The Cariyāpiṭaka (Basket of Conduct) ends: “There was no one equal to me in truth- this was my perfection36 of Truth.” Why was the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be), who had loved the homeless life for thousands of lives, unhappy in it in this one? Because nobody who is not yet enlightened is steady.

"For only seven days did I live the holy life gladly, and for more than fifty years unwillingly. By this truth may the poison be destroyed." The boy shook himself, stood up and was well.

Dīpāyana Yaññadatta his father and mother the snake speaks the truth about himself bitten by the snake “There was no one equal to me in truth- this was my perfection of Truth.”

Small matters. Truthfulness is also keeping one’s word about little things, such as appointments. Even small children notice whether a person does what he says. If a person gets into the habit of small lies, lying becomes easy and he stops seeing that it is wrong. If he keeps to the truth, truthfulness becomes natural to him, and he can see the danger of akusala (bad states) at the very moment a lie is about to be told. The perfection of truthfulness has to be developed together with paññā (wisdom), and with the next perfection, adhiṭṭhāna (determination37).

Chapter 8. Adhiṭṭhāna (determination)

“When the charioteer Sunanda was digging the hole, the Bodhisatta thought, ‘This is my time for effort.’”

Adhiṭṭhāna (determination1) is the firm resolve to reach the four noble truths, even though the way is long and will take an endlessly long time. The ancient texts say it means the firm determination to develop the ten perfections2.

Adhiṭṭhāna (determination) What it is resolving upon the ten perfections What it does overcomes their opposites being unshakeable3 in that task How it shows itself What it needs the ten perfections themselves Why it is needed. Kusala citta (good consciousness4) arises5, and shortly afterwards akusala citta (bad consciousness) arises. Sometimes there is determination for good, but when a bad moment comes and pushes towards something bad, the good is easily given up. That is why firm determination is needed. A person who is in love with pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches will want them again and again, and will not be inclined6 to develop the perfections at all. Wise Temiya. This is the life in which the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) developed determination to the highest degree. It is told in the Mūgapakkha Jātaka (birth story number 538). He was the son of the king of Kāsi, and people called him Temiya, which means wet, because a great shower of rain fell on the day he was born.

After sixteen years of silence: "This is my time for effort."

the unlucky chariot

Temiya Sunanda the charioteer the edge of the forest lifts the chariot like a toy digs the hole “He seized the back of the chariot and lifted it up as if it were a toy-cart for children.”

King Kāsirājā ruled in Vārāṇasī (a city in India). He had sixteen thousand wives, but none of them had a child. His chief queen, Candādevī, lived a good life. On the full-moon day she kept the Uposatha (observance7 day) rules and made an act of truth: “If I have never transgressed8 sīla, may by this assertion of truth a son be borne to me.” Then the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was conceived.

When the prince was one month old, the king sat with the baby on his hip. Just then four robbers were brought in to be sentenced, and the king gave each of them a terrible punishment. When the baby heard his father pass those sentences, he was shaken. He was afraid of doing such deeds9 himself and being reborn10 in hell.

The next day he lay under the white umbrella of royalty and remembered his past lives: a heaven, before that hell, and before that a life as king in this very city. He thought: “I do not need the kingdom. How can I escape from this house of robbers?” A goddess who lived in the umbrella, and who had been his mother in a former life, told him the way: pretend to be dumb, crippled and deaf. From that day he did.

His parents could see none of the signs of a child who is dumb, deaf or crippled. So they began to test him. For a whole day they gave him no milk, but hungry as he was, he made no sound. For years they tried him with cakes, sweets, fruit and toys. Then they tried fear: fire, a wild elephant, snakes, a man waving a sword. He showed no fear, because he thought the danger of hell was a thousand times more fearful. They made deafening noise with conches11 and drums. They smeared him with molasses12 and laid him where flies swarmed. They put pans of burning coals under his bed. For sixteen years they tested him, and he did not change his mind. At sixteen they dressed him like a son of the gods and sent the most graceful women to tempt him. He held his breath so that they could not touch him, and they ran away saying he must be a yakkha (a spirit), not a man.

At last the king called the fortune-tellers13, who said that the boy was a person of ill luck, a danger to the king. The king ordered that the boy be taken out by the back gate and buried in the charnel14 ground. When Temiya heard this he rejoiced15: the wish he had held for so long was about to come true.

Queen Candādevī asked the king to give the kingdom to her son. The king refused. She asked for seven years, then six, five, four, three, two, one; then seven months, down to one; then seven days. To seven days the king agreed. So the prince was crowned and led around the city on an elephant. For five nights his mother begged him: “O Temiya, I did not sleep for sixteen years, I have wept because of you, my child, so that my eyes have become swollen and my heart is pierced with sorrow. I know that you are not cripple, deaf and dumb, do not make me utterly destitute16.” He did not answer.

On the sixth day the king ordered the charioteer17 Sunanda to take the boy at dawn and bury him. In the morning the charioteer carried the prince down, and the queen collapsed with a cry. Temiya thought: if I do not speak, she will die of sorrow. And then: if I speak, my sixteen years will be wasted; if I keep silent, it will be for the good of myself and of my parents. He kept silent.

The chariot18 went to the edge of a forest. The charioteer took a spade and began to dig. Temiya thought: “This is my time for effort.” He rubbed his hands and feet, stepped down from the chariot, and found he had strength enough to walk a hundred leagues. He lifted the chariot by its back as if it were a toy. Then he taught the charioteer: “You are dependent on me, the son of the king. If you bury me in the forest, you will commit evil. It is as if a person who sits or lies in the shade of a tree will not break the branches.” The king was the tree, the prince was the branch, and the charioteer was the traveller resting in its shade. Sunanda begged him to come home. Temiya told him about his past lives and his fear of hell, and said he would become a recluse19 (a person who leaves home to train the mind). Sunanda wanted to become a recluse too. Temiya said: “O, charioteer, take the chariot back and return after you have paid your debts, because a recluse should not have debts, as is the exhortation20 of all hermits21.”

Sunanda told the king everything, and the king set out with his whole army to see his son. Temiya was living happily in a hut in the forest. The king begged him to come and rule. He refused, and taught the king the Dhamma (the Buddha’s teaching) until the king felt saṃvega (urgency22) and wanted to become a recluse too, together with the queen and many of the court. The Buddha said that the goddess in the umbrella was Uppalavaṇṇā, the charioteer was Sāriputta, and wise Temiya was himself.

Wanting is not resolving. The book tells of a person who studied the Dhamma (the teaching), thought about the long cycle of birth and death, and longed for rebirth to end. But he took no interest in developing satipaṭṭhāna (mindfulness23 of realities24). Wanting the end of rebirth is not the same as being firm in one’s determination to develop paññā (wisdom).

Four firm foundations. The commentary25 names four adhiṭṭhāna dhamma (foundations), basic to all the perfections:

1. Sacca (truthfulness26). Firmness in truth, even in small matters, such as keeping an appointment. A person firm in truth stays truthful even when his life is in danger. 2. Cāga (giving up). Not only giving things away, but giving up kilesa (defilements27). This includes guarding the six doors: the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body and mind. The Venerable Sāriputta, when a monk28 falsely accused him, felt no ill will29. He said he was like a duster, which wipes up everything, clean and foul, without disgust. 3. Upasama (calm). Not being disturbed by sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches. 4. Paññā (wisdom). Gained by listening to the teaching, considering it, and asking questions. Someone who thinks that listening once or twice will free him from the cycle of birth and death does not yet

have firm determination.

The great resolve. A person who aspires30 to become a Sammāsambuddha (a fully enlightened31 Buddha) needs extreme dedication and strong desire. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) showed it in his life as Sumedha: when people were clearing a road for the Buddha Dīpaṅkara and it was not ready, Sumedha threw himself down in the mud so that the Buddha could walk on him. If such a person heard that only one who could cross a whole world full of water by the strength of his arms could become a Buddha, he would not shrink away. Because of the Buddha’s great compassion32, nobody now has to do such things. The teaching is here to be listened to.

Quiz 4 (chapters 7 and 8)

The answers are at the back.

1. Deceitful speech is compared in the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets) to bean soup. Why? (a) because beans are a holy food (b) because when a person speaks a great deal, some deceptive words may be mixed in, like hard uncooked beans among the cooked ones (c) because lies taste bad (d) because soup is served first 2. At the First Council, why did the Venerable Ānanda begin with the words evaṃ me sutaṃ (thus have I heard)? 3. Finish the Buddha’s verse at Gayā: “Not by water is one pure, tho’ many folk bathe here. In whom is … “ (a) gold and silver, he is pure (b) truth and dhamma, he is pure and he’s a brāhmin (c) a strong body, he is pure (d) many offerings, he is pure 4. Chapter 9. Mettā (loving-kindness)

“Mettā is like the attitude of a mother towards her child who is still a baby and needs her loving care to grow up.”

Mettā (loving-kindness1) is wishing for the welfare of living beings2. In the Abhidhamma it is the cetasika (mental factor3) adosa (non-hate), the reality4 that is freedom from anger. When mettā (loving-kindness) arises5, there is at that moment no hate and no aversion6 at all.

Mettā (loving-kindness) What it is promoting the welfare of living beings What it does provides for their welfare, or removes resentment7 How it shows itself kindliness8 What it needs seeing the agreeable side of beings Why it comes after determination. Loving-kindness follows determination9 in the list of ten because it is loving-kindness that carries out the determination to work for the welfare of others. That work goes on steadily only when determination is unshakeable10. The one that is forgotten. A person may feel that he has already given enough, kept the rules well enough, is patient and speaks the truth. But has he developed mettā (loving-kindness) as much as the others? It is easy to forget to help, again and again, and to help strangers as readily as friends. If the wish to help others is weak, the reason should be looked for. Is it conceit11? Is it the thought that helping is a waste of time? Is it worrying about what the other person will think? The book says that what another person thinks of us concerns only him, not us.
